comments.author: @barbaranostrand4214
comments.text: MEH! Nevada became a state in 1864 years after the Civil War began. Please check your history before recording presentations. Also, the constitutional status of states is rather different from the constitutional status of provinces. Until Trudeau I, Canada was a self-governing British Colony which could be abolished by a majority vote in the British House of Commons. Meanwhile, the US Revolution constituted the original 13 states as 13 independent nations. Adoption of the US Constitution only partially ceded sovereignty to the Union. This is enshrined not only in the original language of the Constitution which delegates powers to the Federal Government, but is reaffirmed by the tenth amendment. An interesting feature of Canadian provincial history is that provinces have been merged together after one of them went bankrupt as is the case with British Columbia. Finally, Canada was created as a federal government pretty much at the same time as completion of the Canadian transcontinental railroad which facilitated larger local government. Completion of the railroad was a major factor in holding the provinces together at all.

comments.author: @steveempire4625
comments.text: Assuming you broke down Canadian provinces into 50 same-population districts like the US, it would be every 7 districts. The vast majority of these "states" would be in the cities, with only a handful resembling US state sizes. Or, you could split up Canada according to its Senate allocations (105) divided by 2. So, for example, Ontario would have 12 states and BC would have 3. But in my humble opinion, the Canadian Senate is ridiculous in its overrepresentation of smaller provinces. One of the problems with just looking at the territorial expansion of Canada is the continual reorganization of the provinces. Unlike the US where once a state becomes a state, its borders are fixed, that's not the case with Canada, with provinces changing their borders frequently.
